transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-02
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jules Park (Redwood Solutions), Priya Desai (Helix CTO), Marco Ruiz (Helix Platform), Lena O'Neill (Helix SRE), Tom Baxter (Helix Procurement)

Summary:
Quick walkthrough of Redwood's segmentation and quota controls focused on org vs project key patterns, policy routing, and guardrail examples for mixed hosted/dedicated footprints. Customer raised multi-team fairness, burst behavior, and audit requirements. Agreed next steps: pricing, security docs, PoC kickoff.

Topics Covered:
- Org / project API key strategy and naming conventions
- Concurrency & token quotas, burst windows
- Sticky routing and sticky fallback to hosted variants
- Observability: per-key latency/cost breakdowns and audit logs
- Security: VPC/private control plane, KMS, SSO, SOC2 concerns
- PoC goals and success metrics

Action Items (captured here, also in metadata):
- Redwood to send pricing + SLA draft
- SE to produce routing examples and policy templates
- Helix to confirm pilot teams and datasets

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hi everyone good afternoon — thanks for joining, we'll do a 40-ish minute run through focused on segmentation and quota controls and leave time for Q&A. Samir's gonna drive the console parts, I'll cover high level and pricing.
[00:18] Priya Desai: Hi, thanks. Quick note, we're evaluating for multiple teams, two internal AI teams and product infra, so isolation is kind of our top ask.
[00:28] Samir Patel: Great, totally hear that. We'll show examples for per-org and per-project keys, and also how you can carve concurrency slices for teams so they don't step on each other.
[00:40] Marco Ruiz: We have bursty jobs — batch embeddings at night and steady low-latency chat during day. How do you avoid a big embed job trashing chat latency?
[00:52] Samir Patel: Two levers — routing + priority lanes. You can route embeddings to dedicated pools, or set a lower priority queue with throttles and a separate concurrency reserve for chat. There's also automatic fallback to hosted lower-cost variants if your dedicated pool is saturated.
[01:15] Lena O'Neill: Is that the sticky routing thing? I read about sticky in the docs — what is sticky exactly?
[01:22] Alex Chen: Sticky routing means once a key is mapped to a pool or lane, subsequent requests preferentially go there to keep KV cache locality and reduce cold starts. But we also support sticky timeouts and eviction so you can rebalance.
[01:36] Tom Baxter: From procurement standpoint we need hard limits too — not just soft. Can you enforce monthly token quotas and kill keys when they hit the limit?
[01:47] Samir Patel: Yes, you can set both soft throttles and hard caps per key/org. Hitting a hard cap returns a documented 429-like error with reason code; soft throttles attempt graceful shedding and queueing.
[02:02] Priya Desai: About audit logs — we need per-request audit trails for compliance team, and retention for 12 months. Is that supported on Private?
[02:12] Alex Chen: On Private deployments we support long-term audit retention and direct KMS integrations. For hosted we have export hooks to push logs to your cloud storage — retention is configurable with add-on packages.
[02:26] Marco Ruiz: Can we see a quick demo of defining a policy?
[02:30] Samir Patel: Yep, switch to my screen — opening Redwood Console.
[02:36] [screen share noise] Samir Patel: Here in the Console under Policies, you can create a new rate slice. I'll name this 'platform-chat-reserve' and set concurrency to 50 and burst window to 5k tokens over 60 seconds.
[02:56] Priya Desai: Those numbers, are they per-project key or per-org?
[03:01] Samir Patel: You can scoping at both levels. In this example I'm binding it to a project key under the org 'helix-prod'. If you'd rather allocate at org level we can use project selectors to carve out sub-slices.
[03:18] Lena O'Neill: How does billing count when you have sticky routing to a dedicated pool — is it charged to the pool owner or the org?
[03:27] Alex Chen: Billing attribution is token-level; you can map spending to orgs and projects in the Console. For Dedicated pools we separate infrastructure charge and per-token service charge so finance can reconcile.
[03:40] Marco Ruiz: Any built-in protections for noisy neighbors with embeddings? We tried other vendors and embeddings still cause degradation.
[03:48] Samir Patel: We have KV-prefetching for large prefix workloads and auto-batching knobs. For embeddings we recommend routing those to GPU-reserved pools with separate preemption policy and a quota that prevents them from consuming chat reserve.
[04:07] [00:04:07 ambient: someone shuffling papers]
[04:12] Alex Chen: Quick aside on SSO and RBAC — console supports SAML SSO and fine-grained roles. You can map keys to service accounts and assign RBAC so only certain users can create or assign rate slices.
[04:27] Priya Desai: Do you support time-based policies? Some of our teams need higher concurrency during business hours only.
[04:34] Samir Patel: Yes, scheduled policies are supported — you can use timezone-aware windows so chat gets higher reserve 9–5 and embeddings backfill at night.
[04:45] Tom Baxter: For the private deployment, is the control plane hosted by Redwood or customer-managed? We need control plane inside our VPC if possible.
[04:54] Alex Chen: We offer both: a customer-managed control plane deployed into your VPC and a hosted control plane with private peering. For full air-gapped on-prem we ship a bundle that includes the control plane binaries.
[05:07] Marco Ruiz: Any gotchas around KMS? We use an HSM with external key wrap.
[05:13] Samir Patel: Our Private offering can integrate with your KMS/HSM; you can bring your own keys. Hosted integrates with major cloud KMS providers and we support envelope encryption.
[05:25] Priya Desai: Let's walk through a failure scenario — say dedicated pool drops, how do you maintain availability for our customer-facing chat?
[05:34] Alex Chen: There are automated fallbacks: at the policy level you can define fallback model variants (smaller/quantized) and fallback routing to hosted pools in a different region. There's also circuit-breakers per-key and a canary rollouts for model upgrades.
[05:50] Lena O'Neill: How visible is fallback? We need events in our own monitoring when fallback happens.
[05:56] Samir Patel: We emit events to webhook or to your SIEM and Console shows a fallback timeline per key. You can also add tracing hooks to correlate request-level spans.
[06:10] [06:10 noise — someone says "uh-huh"]
[06:18] Alex Chen: Let's demo a policy template for multi-tenant fairness — I'll pull up the 'fairshare' template.
[06:25] Samir Patel: This template uses an allocation ratio across projects within an org and enforces a minimum guarantee plus a shared burst pool. It also rebalances every minute to reflect active usage.
[06:40] Marco Ruiz: Does rebalancing cause abrupt token rejections?
[06:44] Samir Patel: We smooth rebalancing — there's a ramp window, so limits change gradually; instant hard caps are only when admins set a hard cap.
[06:53] Priya Desai: Can we pin a model to a policy? Example: product team wants model-x for completion but others can use model-y.
[06:59] Alex Chen: Yes, policy bindings can include model selectors so you can pin model versions per lane. That way if model-x is expensive it stays isolated.
[07:10] Marco Ruiz: How do you manage secret rotation for project keys at scale?
[07:15] Samir Patel: We support rolling keys and staged rotation — you can create a new key and assign it, then retire the old key after a drain period. There's an API to automate it.
[07:26] Tom Baxter: Any limits on number of project keys? We have hundreds of services that will each want a key.
[07:33] Alex Chen: No hard limit in our platform; we do advise namespace conventions and tag keys for billing. Performance-wise thousands of keys is fine — we've seen mid-enterprise customers with many thousands.
[07:46] [07:46 someone typing]
[07:52] Priya Desai: About observability — can we break down cost by route and feature? Example: tokens used for re-ranking vs chat vs embeddings.
[07:59] Samir Patel: Yes, Console has route-level breakdowns and token categorization. You can export to BI tooling and we've got a cost-allocations API.
[08:13] Lena O'Neill: For the PoC, we'll want sample dashboards and maybe a synthetic load test to validate latency.
[08:20] Alex Chen: Absolutely — we can provide a benchmark harness and a shared spreadsheet so we can define targets (p95 latency, token throughput).
[08:30] Marco Ruiz: Can the PoC run with a mix of hosted and dedicated?
[08:34] Samir Patel: Yes, mixed-deployment pilots are common. We can route production traffic to dedicated and shadow a subset to hosted or vice versa.
[08:44] Priya Desai: Security: do you publish penetration test reports?
[08:49] Alex Chen: We share SOC2 reports under NDA, and we have pen test summaries. For Private on-prem we'll coordinate scope with your security team.
[08:59] Tom Baxter: Pricing question — how do you price dedicated pools vs hosted?
[09:04] Alex Chen: Dedicated is a combination of reserved infra (monthly commitment) plus per-token service fees. Hosted is purely per-token with tiered discounts at volume. We can model a blended rate for your usage mix.
[09:18] [09:18 pause]
[09:22] Samir Patel: I'll show an example of a policy JSON you can apply via API — this one enforces 60 concurrent requests, 10k token burst, and binds to project keys matching 'team-*'.
[09:36] Marco Ruiz: Is that policy portable to Private?
[09:39] Samir Patel: Yes the policy schema is the same across Hosted/Dedicated/Private — that's a core design point so infra teams don't need to rewrite rules.
[09:50] Priya Desai: Any examples of noisy neighbor mitigations in the wild?
[09:55] Samir Patel: We had a customer in payments — they used per-project min guarantees and a shared ephemeral pool; when they hit sustained load we suggested offloading heavy batch jobs to a separate queue and set a lower priority so real-time lanes stayed responsive.
[10:15] Lena O'Neill: Could you show the API call that returns current per-key quotas and usage?
[10:20] Samir Patel: Sure — curl to /v1/keys/{key}/usage returns a JSON with current concurrency, tokens used in window, and policy bindings.
[10:31] [10:31 brief overlap — "yeah" and "okay"]
[10:35] Alex Chen: I'll also note you can set webhook alerts for thresholds so SREs get paged.
[10:42] Priya Desai: Great. Procurement — what's the minimum commitment for Dedicated?
[10:47] Alex Chen: Typical minimum is 3 months for pilot reserved capacity; enterprise contracts can be annual. We'll include options in the pricing sheet.
[10:56] Marco Ruiz: Regarding KMS and key access logs — we need to show auditors that keys were rotated and who triggered actions.
[11:04] Samir Patel: Audit logs include actor, action, and resource; you can integrate with your SIEM and we can retain for the retention window you need.
[11:16] Priya Desai: Back to quotas — can we have hierarchical quotas? Org level limited to X tokens and projects under that have separate allocations?
[11:24] Samir Patel: Yes hierarchical quotas are supported. You can set org cap and then carve project slices that sum to less than or equal org cap or allow overflow into a shared buffer.
[11:38] [11:38 ambient phone vibrate]
[11:42] Alex Chen: Let's talk failure modes when quotas are hit — we support customizable responses: fail-fast 429, queue with retry-after headers, or redirect to degraded-model endpoints.
[11:55] Lena O'Neill: Do you support per-request metadata so we can tag requests for billing and debug?
[12:01] Samir Patel: Yes request metadata headers are supported and are reflected in the observability pipeline.
[12:09] Priya Desai: Competitors — we are also talking to Anthropic and evaluating an in-house proxy. How does Redwood differentiate?
[12:18] Alex Chen: Two things: unified policy and runtime across deployment modes, and deep observability with cost attribution down to route. We focus on production economics and predictable SLAs.
[12:31] Tom Baxter: Ok, last question from procurement — who signs the DPA and how long does security review typically take?
[12:38] Alex Chen: DPAs are standard; security review can be 2–4 weeks depending on scope for private deployments. We'll put timelines in the SOW.
[12:48] [12:48 pause while screen is switched]
[12:55] Samir Patel: Wrapping up — proposed pilot: 4-week PoC with two teams (chat and embeddings), mixed hosted/dedicated, success metrics: p95 latency < 200ms for chat, embedding throughput 50k tokens/minute, no >1% token error rate.
[13:15] Priya Desai: Sounds reasonable. We'll confirm team names.
[13:19] Alex Chen: Great — next steps in the notes. Any final Qs?
[13:24] Marco Ruiz: One tiny ask — can policy templates be exported as Terraform?
[13:29] Samir Patel: We have an infra-as-code exporter for Terraform and Helm for Private.
[13:36] Priya Desai: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[13:40] Alex Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up with pricing and docs.
[13:44] [call ends]

Notes on transcript: The auto-transcription had a few mis-heard product words (e.g., 'KV cache' became 'K-V cash' in places) — we've left originals unchanged from the raw export where present.
